subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: Note to parents, Nursery B. Chinmay, five, changes language without being asked. At pick-up he told Ajji in Marathi, "Mala bhook lagli." Two minutes later he asked his friend Sameer in Hindi, "Kal khelenge?" When I said, "Good afternoon, Chinmay," he answered, "Good afternoon, Sir," and showed me his drawing. He seems to sense what each person expects. I have not corrected him or asked him to choose one language. I told his Ajji that his switching is normal and healthy. Manoj, class teacher

qa.q: What did Chinmay say to Ajji at pick-up?
qa.a: Chinmay told Ajji in Marathi, "Mala bhook lagli."

qa.q: How does Chinmay seem to feel switching languages for each listener?
qa.a: Chinmay seems comfortable and at ease, switching language without being asked and even showing the teacher his drawing.

qa.q: What choice did the teacher make about Chinmay's switching, and why?
qa.a: The teacher did not correct him or ask him to pick one language, and told Ajji it is normal and healthy, so Chinmay can keep using all three.

qa.q: How might Ajji have felt when she heard the teacher's words?
qa.a: Probably reassured and proud, since the teacher said the switching is normal and healthy.

grounding: A child speaks one language to a grandparent, another to a friend and English at school without being told, sensing which language each person expects.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: In a village near Warangal, Hafsa, five, ran from her Nani's veranda to the lane. To Nani she said in Urdu, "Nani, paani do." To her friend Mahima at the well she called in Telugu, "Raa, aadukundam!" When the school van came, the teacher said, "Good morning, Hafsa," and Hafsa answered, "Good morning, Miss," and climbed in. Mahima giggled and shouted "Bye bye!" in English, and Hafsa waved from the window, already humming a Telugu song.

qa.q: Which language did Hafsa speak to Nani?
qa.a: Hafsa spoke Urdu to Nani, saying, "Nani, paani do."

qa.q: What might Hafsa be feeling as she hums a Telugu song in the van?
qa.a: Hafsa is probably happy and at ease, moving comfortably between the languages of her day.

qa.q: What choice does Hafsa make when the teacher greets her, and what does it show?
qa.a: Hafsa answers in English, "Good morning, Miss," showing that she senses which language the teacher expects without being told.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel about the languages she shares with Hafsa?
qa.a: Probably playful and at ease, since she giggles and shouts "Bye bye!" in English to her friend.

grounding: A child speaks one language to a grandparent, another to a friend and English at school without being told, sensing which language each person expects.

passage:
Monday. Sahil, five, climbed onto Dadu Anirban's lap and chattered in Bengali about the pigeons. Nobody had told him to.
Wednesday. At the park, Sahil ran up to his friends and yelled in Hindi, "Chalo, pakdam-pakdai!" He didn't use a single Bengali word.
Friday. At school, his teacher asked, "What did you do this week, Sahil?" He answered in careful English: "I played catch and I saw pigeons."
That evening Mumma told Dadu. Dadu laughed. "He knows who speaks what better than we do!" Sahil, busy with his blocks, just said, "Dadu, dekho!"

qa.q: What did Sahil chatter about in Bengali?
qa.a: He chattered in Bengali about the pigeons.

qa.q: How did Dadu feel when he heard about Sahil's switching?
qa.a: Dadu felt amused and proud, laughing that Sahil knows who speaks what better than they do.

qa.q: What could Sahil's family do to keep all his languages strong?
qa.a: They could keep speaking Bengali with Dadu, let him play in Hindi, and support his English at school without correcting the switching.

qa.q: How might Sahil's teacher see him?
qa.a: His teacher probably sees a child who speaks English carefully and clearly in class, unaware of all his other languages.

grounding: Over one week, a young child switches languages for his grandfather, friends and school without being told, sensing which each expects.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
The wedding hall was so loud Parveen, five, could barely hear herself. Her mother was helping in the kitchen.
She tugged her Nani's dupatta and said in Urdu, "Nani, mujhe pani chahiye." Nani brought water.
Then her cousin's friend Shalini, who only spoke English, asked her something. Parveen answered, "My shoes are hurting," in English, without missing a beat.
A minute later, she was shouting in Hindi to the other children, "Idhar aao, cake aa gaya!"
Shalini's mother was amazed. "How does she know who speaks what?"
Parveen shrugged and ran after the cake.

qa.q: What did Parveen tell Shalini in English?
qa.a: Parveen answered, "My shoes are hurting."

qa.q: How did Shalini's mother feel watching Parveen?
qa.a: Shalini's mother felt amazed at how easily Parveen switched languages for each person.

qa.q: What does this scene suggest adults can do to support children like Parveen?
qa.a: Adults can let children switch freely and admire it, since children quickly sense which language a person expects.

qa.q: What might it be like for Shalini to talk to Parveen?
qa.a: Shalini probably finds it easy and comfortable, because Parveen speaks to her in English.

grounding: In a noisy wedding hall, a young child switches between Urdu, English and Hindi for each listener without being told.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
Avni, five, lived on the third floor of an old building in Ahmedabad. With her Ba she spoke only Gujarati: "Ba, rotli aapo." With Joseph from downstairs, whose family was from Kerala, she spoke Hindi. At school, she answered her teacher in English.
One day Joseph came up to play. Ba asked him something in Gujarati. Avni turned to Joseph and translated into Hindi, then turned back to Ba and answered for him in Gujarati.
Ba laughed. "Our little translator."
Avni looked proud. Then she told Joseph, in Hindi, "Now we eat thepla."

qa.q: What did Avni do when Ba asked Joseph something in Gujarati?
qa.a: Avni turned to Joseph and translated into Hindi, then answered for him in Gujarati.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when Ba called her a little translator?
qa.a: Avni felt proud.

qa.q: What could adults do to support Avni's languages?
qa.a: They could praise her switching as Ba did, and keep using Gujarati, Hindi and English with her.

qa.q: What is it like for Joseph to have Avni as a friend?
qa.a: Joseph can join in easily because Avni translates for him, which likely makes him feel included.

grounding: A young child speaks Gujarati to her grandmother, Hindi to a friend and English at school, switching and even translating without being told.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
"Paati, saapadu ready-aa?" Ramesh called, dropping his bag.
"Ready, kanna. Wash your hands."
At the gate Pooja waved. "Ramesh! Khelne chalo!"
"Ruko, pehle khana!" he shouted back.
His father looked up from the newspaper. "And what did you tell Miss Grace today?"
"I said, 'May I go to the toilet, please?'" Ramesh answered in careful English, then grinned.
"Who taught you when to use which?"
Ramesh shrugged, mouth full of rice. "Nobody. I just know."

qa.q: What did Ramesh say to Miss Grace?
qa.a: He said, "May I go to the toilet, please?"

qa.q: What does Ramesh's shrug and "I just know" suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels relaxed and confident, switching languages so naturally that it does not feel like work to him.

qa.q: How could his family encourage this skill?
qa.a: They can keep speaking each language with him and show interest, as his father does, so he stays proud of switching.

qa.q: What is it like for Pooja when Ramesh answers her in Hindi?
qa.a: Pooja probably feels at ease and included, since he uses the language they share when playing.

grounding: It illustrates a young child who uses Tamil with a grandparent, Hindi with a friend and English at school, sensing each listener's language without being told.
